category.text: $course$/Game Theory/Chapter 05 - Zero-Sum Games and the Minimax Theorem (Quiz)

generalfeedback.text: The defining property is that in every cell the payoffs sum to zero (or, equivalently up to a harmless constant shift, to the same constant). It is a property of every cell, not of the equilibrium alone.

answer.text: The two players' payoffs sum to zero in every cell
The equilibrium payoffs are both zero

feedback.text: The value can be any number, as in the example with v = 1.

answer.text: Neither player can gain from the game

feedback.text: One player can have a strictly positive value.

questiontext.text:
Player 1's payoffs (player 2 receives the negative of each):

XYZ
A435
B216
C307

What is player 1's maximin value?

generalfeedback.text: Row minima are 3 (row A), 1 (row B) and 0 (row C). The maximin is the largest of these, 3, achieved by playing A. Column maxima are 4, 3, 7, so the minimax is also 3 - the game has a saddle point at (A, Y) and its value is 3.

questiontext.text: Using the same matrix, what is the minimax value?

generalfeedback.text: Column maxima are 4, 3, 7. The minimax is their smallest, 3, at column Y. Since maximin = minimax = 3, the game has a value of 3 in pure strategies and (A, Y) is a saddle point.

questiontext.text: In any finite two-player zero-sum game, the maximin value is always less than or equal to the minimax value.

generalfeedback.text: True, and it holds before any mixing is allowed. Intuitively, being able to move second cannot hurt. The minimax theorem says the two coincide once mixed strategies are permitted.

questiontext.text: Player 1's payoffs: Top gives \(3\) against Left and \(-1\) against Right; Bottom gives \(-2\) against Left and \(4\) against Right. What is the value of this zero-sum game?

generalfeedback.text: Player 1 mixes with probability \(p\) on Top so that the two columns are equal: \(5p - 2 = 4 - 5p\) gives \(p = 0.6\), and the payoff is \(3(0.6) - 2(0.4) = 1\). Player 2 mixes with \(q = 0.5\) on Left and gets the same number, so \(v = 1\).

questiontext.text: In the same 2x2 game, with what probability does player 1 play Top in the optimal mixed strategy? Give a decimal.

generalfeedback.text: Equalising the value of the two columns for player 1: \(3p - 2(1-p) = -p + 4(1-p)\), i.e. \(5p - 2 = 4 - 5p\), so \(p = 0.6\).

name.text: C05 Q7 - What is special about zero-sum

questiontext.text: Which property holds in every finite two-player zero-sum game but fails in general games?

generalfeedback.text: All equilibria of a zero-sum game give the same payoffs (the value) and equilibrium strategies are interchangeable, so there is no equilibrium-selection problem. In Battle of the Sexes, by contrast, different equilibria give very different payoffs and mixing strategies across equilibria gives a non-equilibrium.

answer.text: All Nash equilibria give the same payoffs, and equilibrium strategies are interchangeable

feedback.text: In zero-sum games every outcome is trivially efficient, so this does not distinguish anything useful about equilibria.

answer.text: Every player has a dominant strategy

questiontext.text: The value and optimal strategies of a finite two-player zero-sum game can be computed in polynomial time by linear programming.

generalfeedback.text: True. Each player's problem is a linear program and the two are duals of each other, so the minimax theorem is a form of LP strong duality. This contrasts sharply with general two-player games, where finding a Nash equilibrium is PPAD-complete.
